name: PT FKS Multi Agro Tbk

frontmatter.title: FKS Multi Agro: the spread between the price and the business
frontmatter.summary: FKS Multi Agro trades and distributes the food and feed ingredients Indonesia consumes on a mid-single-digit gross spread, plus port logistics. At 0.6x book and 4.8x EV/EBITDA the market sits between our post-haircut bear and base. The business is worth Rp471 after the illiquidity discount, but the register cannot carry a position. Add, unactionable.
thesis: A spread business, not a planter: US$1,174.4m of revenue at a 5.4% gross margin, with trading and distribution at US$1,147.1m of the total — earnings follow tonnage and the rupiah spread, and commodity price moves pass through revenue rather than margin [S4][S2].

The FY2025 profit trough was manufactured: a US$5.4m impairment of supplier advances and an effective tax rate above the statutory rate cut parent profit to US$8.7m; strip the impairment and operating profit is US$24.9m on our restated D&A of US$10.9m, and first-half 2026 gross margin already runs above the FY2025 average [S2][S0].

The shares are not investable at size, and that comes before the view: daily traded value is IDR96.1m against the constitution floor of two billion rupiah a day, the engine records the name as not investable, and the 30.0% haircut is a valuation adjustment rather than a cure for the exit [S0].
Value: DCF at a 10.0% WACC gives Rp486 a share and peer-median EV/EBITDA gives Rp511; after the house illiquidity haircut the target is Rp471, 15.0% total return including the dividend [S0].

Governance is the discount and the risk: 79.1% control, US$632.3m of goods and services bought from related parties against cost of revenues, and a standing shareholder authority to pledge assets and give corporate guarantees above 50.0% of net assets to affiliates [S2].
What would change our mind: two consecutive quarters of gross margin back at the FY2024 level, or related-party terms that move purchases away from market prices [S2][S6].

catalysts.event: Bapanas review of the HAP ceiling on imported soybeans; any change resets the achievable spread
FY2026 audited accounts: gross margin, whether the advance impairment repeats, and the related-party purchase share
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend declaration

blocks.text: We initiate on PT FKS Multi Agro at ADD with a target of Rp471, a 15.0% total return from a Rp428 price. The gate comes before the rating. Threemonth average daily traded value is IDR96.1m and the constitution's floor for an Indonesian equity is two billion rupiah a day — some twenty times the traded value here — so the engine records the name as not investable. Market capitalisation and board listing both pass that test; traded value does not, and it is the traded-value limb that binds. We hold no exemption and claim none. **ADD is therefore not an actionable position at this traded value.** The view is a watch-list idea: a fundamental statement about a business whose register cannot carry a fund position until the float trades, with the 30.0% haircut in the target as a valuation adjustment rather than a cure for the exit [S0]. The company is not what its sector label says. It owns no estate and sells no crude palm oil: it imports, warehouses and distributes soybean, soybean meal, flour, sugar and feed ingredients across a national network, and runs port handling and warehousing through subsidiaries [S2][S4]. Trading and distribution is US$1,147.1m of revenue; logistics is US$39.3m and the legacy fish-meal plant US$4.1m [S4][S2].

That mix explains the numbers. Revenue of US$1,174.4m earned a gross profit of US$63.3m — a 5.4% spread — and an operating profit of US$24.9m [S2]. When commodity prices fell in FY2025, revenue fell -9.2% while management reports that sales volume of regular products rose; that is the signature of near-complete cost pass-through, and it is why we model a spread and not a price [S2]. Management's own target for 2026 is volume growth plus margin and cost discipline against a slower economy [S2].

The equity has been repriced, and not only by a share register. Split-adjusted, the shares traded between roughly five hundred and fifty and nine hundred rupiah from 2021 to 2023, were frozen at a little over a thousand rupiah for the eight months of 2025 during which the company failed the free-float requirement, were split one-for-ten in September 2025 and reopened at nearly three times that frozen level, and have fallen for fourteen months to Rp428, with the fifty-two-week high at Rp1,715 [S0][S2]. Today's price is below every split-adjusted print we hold, including the level at which the stock was frozen, so the September 2025 reopening was the anomaly and today is the repricing. That matters for the argument: a split changes neither a percentage nor a business, the public line of 10.5% is the same before and after it, and a price this far below the pre-suspension level is a verdict on the business rather than a register artefact [S2]. What the register does explain is amplitude: with 79.1% held by the controlling shareholder and 10.4% by the second five-percent holder, the public line is 10.5% and the exchange's own free-float measure is lower still at 8.6%, so a float this small amplifies both directions and does not discover a price [S0].

Our base case values the operating business at Rp571 a share. The multiple cross-checks bracket it, and the house applies an explicit 30.0% illiquidity haircut because the name trades below the book's turnover floor — never a hidden discount-rate premium [S0]. The three things that move the value are the gross spread, the working-capital cycle that funds it, and whether the group's related-party supply terms stay at market. The spread dominates: a tenth off the assumed gross margin is worth roughly a fifth of the target, and nothing else in the model comes close [S2].

Consolidated food-ingredient trading is a scale game. The gross spread a distributor earns is thin
because the product is a commodity with a published reference price, and the returns come from turning
working capital quickly and from owning the port and warehouse assets that others must rent. The
business therefore looks like a logistics company wearing a trading company's income statement, and it
is valued on spread stability rather than on commodity price direction.

FKS Multi Agro began as a fishery company, listed in 2001, and transformed into the trading and distribution of agricultural commodities for the food and feed chains [S2]. Today it reports three segments. Trading and distribution — food ingredients such as soybean, sugar, wheat flour, rice flour, tapioca and corn flour, FMCG lines for kitchens and snacks, and feed ingredients including soybean and rapeseed meal, corn gluten feed, wheat bran, fishmeal, meat and bone meal and phosphates — contributed US$1,147.1m of FY2025 revenue [S4][S2]. Logistics, at US$39.3m, covers stevedoring and port handling, warehouse lease and management, and trucking in Cilegon and Semarang, supported by an integrated port warehouse with handling capacity of 350,000 metric tonnes and a EURO IV truck fleet [S4]; it is run through PT Nusa Prima Logistik, 65.0% of which the group owns, on US$27.4m of total assets [S2]. Manufacturing, the legacy fish-meal and fish-oil plant, was US$4.1m of revenue, down by more than a third in FY2025 because raw fish was unavailable, and an inter-segment elimination of US$16.1m comes out of the three segment lines — they sum to more than the consolidated total, so it is the elimination and not the manufacturing line that closes the gap [S2].

The operating model is national distribution off strategic ports: the company buys imported agricultural commodities, stores them in bonded and general warehouses, and sells them in bagged and bulk form to feed mills, food processors, tofu and tempe artisans, and through business-to-business and business-to-consumer channels [S2][S4]. Because it takes title, it carries the inventory and the receivable, and because the products are staples with administered reference prices, it earns a percentage spread on a large revenue base rather than a margin on value added. FY2025 revenue of US$1,174.4m produced operating profit of US$24.9m and parent net profit of US$8.7m [S2].

Scale, not pricing power, is the strategy. Management's stated 2026 priorities are sales-volume growth across every segment, margin improvement through tighter cost control and process work, and cash-flow discipline, against an expected economic slowdown [S2]. Capital spending goes into the distribution footprint — the integrated warehouse with automated handling, and the truck fleet — which is maintenance-scale: capex of US$9.9m against revenue of US$1,174.4m [S2][S4]. The company sits in the challenger tier of Indonesian food distribution: it is a meaningful importer and port operator, but the market is served by larger trading houses and by the mills themselves, and the group's own affiliates are simultaneously suppliers and competitors [S2].

Ownership is concentrated and family-group controlled. PT FKS Corporindo Indonesia holds 79.1% of the shares and PT Caturkartika Perdana a further 10.4%, with the public line at 10.5% on the annual report's count and no holder smaller than the reporting threshold broken out [S2]. The two five-percent-plus holders therefore hold a little under nine-tenths between them; the exchange's own free-float measure, which uses a narrower non-affiliate test, is lower at 8.6% [S0]. The ultimate parent is FKS International Investments Pte Ltd in Singapore [S2]. The company employs 852 people [S0]. Its reporting currency is the US dollar, which matters: the traded goods are priced in dollars and the selling prices are rupiah, so the spread carries an embedded FX exposure that the accounts translate [S2].

The addressable business is Indonesian food and feed ingredient distribution: soybean for tofu, tempe and soy sauce; soybean meal and corn gluten feed for poultry feed; wheat and rice flour, sugar and FMCG for retail and food service. Demand is driven by population and protein consumption and is remarkably insensitive to the cycle — which is why the company's revenue fell in FY2025 on price, not on volume [S2]. Supply is imported, so the cost side is set by the world soybean complex and the rupiah, and the selling side is increasingly set by policy.

That policy is the single most important industry variable, and the headroom in it is thin enough to measure. Badan Pangan Nasional sets a Harga Acuan Penjualan ceiling for imported soybeans at the artisan level; in October 2026 the average imported soybean price in Java was 11,573 rupiah a kilogram against a ceiling of 12,000 per kilogram [S6]. That leaves less than four per cent of room between the market price and the cap. Now put the rupiah beside it: the house macro deck has the exchange rate at Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E against Rp18,063/USD spot, a move of the same order as the headroom [S0]. Because the cost of revenues of US$1,111.1m is almost entirely imported, a rupiah depreciation of the size the deck already assumes closes that gap with no change in world prices at all. When the world price rises through the ceiling, the distributor cannot pass it on and the spread compresses; when the price sits below it, the spread normalises. Bapanas also runs a soybean stabilisation programme to keep artisan costs down [S7]. For a company whose largest single product line is soybean, this is a regulated margin, and it is why we do not extend the 2026 margin improvement into the long run.

Our agri deck prices the complex, and it is not benign for a buyer: soybean meal is US$411/t for FY2026E and US$411/t for FY2027E against US$321/t in FY2025A, and soybean oil US$1,557/t against US$1,082/t [S0]. That is the single most important reconciliation in this report, and it is the one a reader should test: an input price rising by more than a quarter between FY2025A and FY2027E cannot be passed through a domestic ceiling that moves by nothing, so the deck's price strength is a spread risk, not a revenue driver. Our revenue line therefore grows on volume and mix, not on the deck's price — and the accounts do not split revenue by product, so we cannot size the soymeal line exactly, only observe that it sits inside a book where US$1,147.1m of US$1,174.4m is trading and distribution [S2]. The offset is that a rising dollar value per tonne lifts the absolute rupiah spread on the same tonnage; the ceiling decides how much of it the distributor keeps. The deck's through-cycle anchors, not its spot prints, are what the DCF should see, and the forecast margin path in section three is set to hold rather than expand.

Competitive position is a narrow moat. The company's advantage is physical: bonded warehousing at strategic ports, the largest integrated facility, a national distribution network and a truck fleet, all of which are expensive to replicate and are what a feed mill or a flour mill would otherwise have to build [S4]. Against that, the product is undifferentiated, switching costs for a feed mill are low, and the group's affiliates are viable alternatives, so supplier and customer bargaining power both bite. Five-forces reading: high buyer power, because feed mills and millers are large and can self-import; high supplier power from the concentrated global trade and from affiliated suppliers that provide more than half of purchases; moderate threat of new entrants, given warehouse capital; low substitution for the product itself; and rivalry disciplined by the reference price. The result is the observed 5.4% gross margin and a return on equity of 5.2% [S2].

External influences to monitor: the rupiah and therefore the dollar cost of imports; the Bapanas reference price and the SPHP programme [S6][S7]; Indonesian import licensing and quota practice on soybean and feed grains; and the freight and port cycle that sets logistics revenue. On the equity side, the IDX regime matters: in September 2026 the exchange revised the criteria for its special monitoring board, aligning them with free float, liquidity and minimum-price rules under the full call auction [S9]. We could not confirm board status positively — the exchange's own site is outside this desk's source registry — and we say so rather than assert either way; the release list of September 2026 that we hold does not name FISH, and the annual report records no notation letter [S8][S2]. The item matters because a special-monitoring listing trades through a full call auction, which would break every entry and exit assumption behind the liquidity discount in section four.

History first, because the data pack misstates it in one decisive place. The pack carries depreciation and amortisation of only about a million dollars for FY2025 — the G&A line alone — where the audited accounts put most of the charge inside cost of revenues, the logistics segment absorbing the larger part. The true total is US$10.9m for FY2025, US$10.2m for FY2024 and US$10.2m for FY2023 [S2][S10]. We restate the history from the filings, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA to US$35.7m. On the restated figure the FY2025 actual multiple is 5.0x EV/EBITDA and the FY2026E forward multiple is 4.8x: the restatement takes the trailing number from above six times to the low fives, and it is the forward year, not the restated actual, that trades at 4.8x [S0].

The same filings correct the operating line. The company reports operating profit of US$24.9m on operating expenses of US$38.4m, against revenue of US$1,174.4m [S2]. Within those expenses sits US$5.4m of impairment of supplier advances — nil in the prior year — alongside higher business-development remuneration; that is the whole of the jump in operating costs and the reason parent profit fell to US$8.7m in a year when gross profit actually rose [S2]. The elevated effective tax rate in FY2025 is the same item at work, since the impairment is not deductible [S2].

Our forecast holds the last actual's economics rather than extrapolating the impairment, but it now carries the third quarter. Revenue is flat in FY2026E — the nine months to September were flat on the prior year, H1 revenue of US$572.3m below the US$583.0m of the prior-year first half and Q3 above — and then grows 4.0% a year on management's volume push and a richer feed and FMCG mix, not on the deck's price: the Bapanas ceiling caps pass-through, as section two sets out. Gross margin is 5.6% in FY2026E, the nine-month actual carried through a fourth quarter at the prior year's rate, and then 5.7%, a modest recovery that still sits below the ceiling-capped path [S6][S11]. Operating costs are held at 3.0% of revenue, the nine-month run-rate; the FY2025 ratio including the impairment, the ratio excluding it, and the first half of 2026 all sit in a narrow band around it [S2][S11].

The honest test of that forecast is the quarter we now hold. Nine-month revenue was US$885.0m and gross profit US$49.5m, against US$572.3m and US$34.7m in the first half; subtract the two and the third quarter is the residual, with a gross margin below both the half-year and the 5.6% we now carry for the year. The payables stretch unwound in that quarter: third-party trade payables fell from US$72.7m in June to US$26.7m in September [S12][S11], so nine-month operating cash flow was an outflow of US$-12.1m against an inflow of US$30.0m in the first half. That is why FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is US$-11.7m and free cash flow to equity US$-15.7m: the earlier FCFE yield was annual-model cash that the third quarter had already spent. The tax charge is not a modelling choice either — nine months of US$8.7m on US$20.4m of pre-tax profit is the rate we now use, and the quarter's own rate is above it. Margin, tax and working capital are calibrated on the nine-month actuals rather than fitted to the first half; the earlier claim that the second-half cost line was the sole swing factor has gone with the full data.

The result is EBITDA of US$41.6m against US$35.7m in FY2025, and parent profit of US$12.9m against US$8.7m [S0][S11]. The step-up is the impairment and the tax rate, not a new business: on FY2025 operating profit plus the impairment, the FY2026E operating profit of US$30.7m is of the same order.

The tax line needs a word because it carries much of the earnings step. The statutory rate is twenty-two per cent; the gap to the 42.8% effective rate we use is explained by non-deductible expenses and deferred-tax adjustments in the LK reconciliation [S2]. The nine-month charge of US$8.7m on US$20.4m matches that rate; the lower rate in the earlier draft was the FY2024 print alone and could not be reconciled with the charge already paid in 2026.

Cash is the honest test of a trading book, and it is now the decisive part of the story. Nine‑month operating cash flow is an outflow of US$-12.1m after the payables unwind; FY2025 operating cash flow was US$19.0m [S2]. Free cash flow to the firm follows the model’s own build: US$24.9m of operating profit taxed at that year’s effective rate, plus US$10.9m of D&A, less US$9.9m of capex and a US$1.5m working‑capital build, gave US$12.6m — which is why the D&A restatement matters twice, once to EBITDA and once to cash [S2]. The gap between profit and operating cash is working capital: US$93.8m of net working capital, 10.5% of revenue, with inventories at US$189.0m and advances to suppliers that nearly doubled to US$32.0m [S2]. Those advances are precisely where the impairment landed, which makes the advance line a monitoring item rather than a footnote. Our forecast keeps working capital at the last actual's ratio and funds it from operations: net debt rises from US$58.1m at the end of FY2025 to US$77.6m at the end of FY2026E as the payables unwind absorbs cash, then falls to US$55.2m by FY2030E without new borrowing, and net debt to EBITDA moves from 1.6x to 1.9x [S0]. The valuation section explains which of those net-debt figures the DCF actually deducts, and why.

Balance-sheet health is adequate rather than strong. Gross debt of US$134.5m against equity of US$168.6m is a debt-to-equity ratio the company reports below one, with a current ratio above one, and the debt is short-dated bank paper [S2]. The guarantee structure is the governance item, and the direction matters: the annual general meeting resolved to approve pledging the company's assets in excess of 50.0% of net assets in a single financial year, in the form of assets and/or corporate guarantees, for facilities granted to the company and/or its subsidiaries and/or **parties affiliated with the company** [S2 p.121]. So the guarantee runs out of FISH towards affiliates, not into FISH from its parent. On the last balance sheet that authority covers more than half of US$168.6m of equity, and the resolution is standing rather than transaction-specific — which is a contingent exposure to the wider group's credit, not a source of support [S2]. We found no source for the cross-guarantee-from-parent wording in our earlier draft and withdraw it.

Capital allocation is a stable payout and reinvestment in the distribution footprint. The dividend out of FY2025 was 14 rupiah a share on the 4,800 million post-split shares, a payout of 43.0% of parent profit, and capex runs below one percent of revenue [S2][S0]. The prior year was larger: 150 rupiah a pre-split share, US$4.4m in total, or half of FY2024 profit [S2 note 22]. There has been no rights issue and no buyback, and the share count is unchanged at 4,800 million after the one-for-ten split [S2].

Earnings-quality flags, from the house screen. Accruals are not the problem — operating cash flow tracks profit over three years once the FY2024 working-capital release is set aside [S2]. The flags are structural: related-party purchases of US$632.3m against cost of revenues, at prices the notes describe as agreed with reference to market prices [S2]; related-party trade payables of US$86.9m, more than half of the payables book [S2]; advances to suppliers of US$32.0m carrying a US$5.4m impairment [S2]; and a tax charge above the statutory rate in the year of a non-deductible loss [S2]. None of these is fabricated cash or fictitious revenue; they are optics-class disclosure items, and they belong in the discount rate rather than in a restatement.

We value a spread business on the cash it produces, discounted at a rate that reflects a thinly traded small cap. The primary method is a ten-year free-cash-flow-to-firm DCF with a 10.0% WACC and 2.0% terminal growth; the cross-checks are peer-median EV/EBITDA and P/BV, which suit a distributor because book value here is largely receivables and inventory marked close to market, and because EBITDA is a clean measure once D&A is correctly taken from the filings [S2].

The cost of capital is built on the macro deck: a 5.1% dollar risk-free rate, a 4.2% mature-market equity risk premium, a 2.5% Indonesia country premium and an unlevered beta of 0.80 levered at a debt-to-market- capitalisation ratio of 1.50 — the leverage ratio is high precisely because the equity has fallen, which is correct arithmetic and a real risk. That gives a cost of equity of 16.7% and, with debt at 7.1% pre-tax, a WACC of 10.0% [S0]. Two rates for one liability, and both are right for their job. The 7.1% in the WACC is the macro deck's dollar risk-free rate plus its corporate debt spread — a forward cost of new money. The 6.5% that capitalises the interest line in section three is what the accounts actually paid on an inherited book of short-dated bank facilities [S2]. They are not interchangeable, and we state the gap rather than net it away: running the WACC on the paid rate would lower it by about a quarter of a point and add roughly thirty rupiah a share, which is disclosed conservatism, not a hidden one. We add no illiquidity premium to the rate: the house prices illiquidity once, as an explicit 30.0% haircut to the target, and the constitution forbids hiding it in the discount rate.

The blended value is Rp571 a share, of which the DCF contributes Rp486. Rolled forward one year at the 16.7% cost of equity and reduced by the 21 rupiah dividend received over that year — a target is a price, so the dividend comes out of it rather than being added — that becomes Rp645 before the 30.0% haircut [S0]. Probability-weighting the three scenarios at their stated odds gives Rp673, and after the same haircut the target is Rp471. The arithmetic is not heroic: free cash flow is US$-11.7m in FY2026E, depressed by the payables unwind, and recovers to US$15.5m in FY2027E as the working-capital ratio stabilises. Terminal value is half the enterprise value (52.0%), which is what a stable-spread distributor with low reinvestment should show. What the model is really doing is capitalising a 3.5% EBITDA margin at a cost of capital a few points above the risk-free rate, on a business whose cash flow is stable and whose reinvestment need is under one percent of revenue.

One line in that bridge must be stated on the engine's basis. The DCF begins on 1 October 2026 and discounts FY2026E only for the remaining quarter, so it deducts the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet net debt, in line with our FY2026E year-end forecast of US$77.6m — debt less cash at that date — not a mid-year estimate and not a deduction for the full forecast year. That September net debt is also our FY2026E year-end forecast of US$77.6m, because the payables stretch unwound inside the third quarter: net debt rose by the whole of that quarter's negative operating cash flow as payables fell. The earlier draft deducted a lower June net debt and told the reader to carry a further deduction for an assumed unwind; both were wrong — the unwind had already happened — and both are removed. There is no further balance-sheet adjustment: the September actual and the forecast year-end agree.

The cross-checks bracket the primary method. EV/EBITDA at Rp511 is the more meaningful cross-check and it sits 5.2% from the DCF, which is what we would expect when the capital structure is stable and the margin is normalised. P/BV at Rp1,007 sits 107.2% above the primary method, and that divergence is a peer-set artefact rather than a signal: the peer medians are upstream planters whose book is a mature estate, whereas FISH earns a 5.2% return on equity and would not deserve a planter's multiple on any fundamental view [S0]. Because it sits above the primary rather than below it, it is a ceiling cross-check, not a floor: we keep it at the house-minimum weight as a second opinion on the asset backing, and the target does not lean on it.

One part of the group is not priced by that spread, and the omission was ours. Logistics is US$39.3m of revenue, run through a 65.0%-owned subsidiary with US$27.4m of total assets and the 350,000 metric tonne integrated port warehouse [S2][S4]. Against a group enterprise value of US$211.1m in the DCF, twice the arm's asset base would be about a quarter of the whole — too large to wave away as immaterial, and the wrong thing to value on a trading multiple. We do not add it: the DCF already capitalises those cash flows, and a sum-of-the-parts would be a cross-check on the same numbers, not a second source of value. It does mean the group's 3.5% EBITDA spread understates the quality of the mix, and it is why the statement that the moat is physical is not just a phrase [S4].

Two parameters carry the result. Gross spread dominates: a change of a tenth in the assumed margin moves the target by roughly a fifth to a quarter, because the spread is the entire operating margin of the business — that is the engine's own gross-margin behaviour, and it is the relationship a reader should use. The cost of capital is second: a quarter of a point on the WACC is worth about thirty rupiah a share. Volume growth, by contrast, is nearly value-neutral because growth consumes working capital at 10.5% of revenue and earns a spread on it — which is why we do not pay for the company's volume ambitions and do not penalise their absence [S2].

A note on the sensitivity block, because it is deliberately absent. The industry template generates it from the crude palm oil benchmark, the rupiah and a mining strip ratio, none of which enters this model; printed here it would show flat columns and imply a precision the business does not have. We have suppressed it rather than fill space. The real sensitivity is the one above: gross spread moves the target by a fifth to a quarter for a tenth of margin, and working capital is the second lever, visible in the FY2026E cash outflow of US$-11.7m when the payables ratio moves back to its September level. A gross-margin grid would be the honest table; the engine does not generate one for this template, and we do not print a dead one in its place.

What the price implies, this time on a like-for-like basis. At Rp428 the market capitalises the equity at IDR2,054.4bn, or 4.8x EV/EBITDA and 8.8x our FY2026E earnings with a 4.9% dividend yield [S0]. Our bear case is Rp485 a share before the illiquidity haircut and, with the same 30.0% the house applies to its target, below today's price rather than at it. The market is therefore not pricing our bear: it sits above the post-haircut bear and below the post-haircut base of Rp471. The earlier claim that the price was our bear "almost to the rupiah" compared a post-haircut price with a pre-haircut value; the arithmetic runs the other way. The engine's reverse-DCF routine is wired to the crude palm oil benchmark, which this company neither buys nor sells, and returns no answer for this name; we have therefore deleted the earlier "working the DCF backwards" sentence rather than report a number the engine did not produce.

That makes the call a closer one, not a weaker one. The bear is a spread below the 5.4% actually delivered in FY2025 and a first half of 2026 running above 5.6%; if the price sits between the post-haircut bear and base, the question is whether a margin below the last two years is more likely than not, and our answer is no — but the margin of safety is thinner than the earlier draft claimed. The bull case that gets there is cash: normalised free cash flow to equity of US$10.9m against dividends of US$5.5m is about double cover at a 9.6% yield on today's market value, while the payout is 43.0% [S0]. A business that throws off nearly a tenth of its market value in free equity cash a year and pays out less than half of it does not need a re-rating to make money — it needs the spread to stop falling. The three sourced drivers of our 15.0% expected return are therefore: the gross spread holding at 5.6% rather than the FY2024 4.1% [S2]; the one-off US$5.4m advance impairment not repeating [S2]; and working capital stabilising at 10.5% of revenue, so that free cash flow from FY2027E funds the dividend without new debt [S2].

The largest risk is regulatory, and the sizing is uncomfortable rather than comfortable. Bapanas sets a ceiling on the price at which imported soybeans may be sold to artisans — 12,000 rupiah a kilogram in October 2026 against a market price of 11,573 — and runs a stabilisation programme alongside it [S6][S7]. That is less than four per cent of headroom. With cost of revenues of US$1,111.1m almost entirely imported and the deck's own rupiah path running from Rp18,063/USD spot to Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E, a currency move smaller than the deck already assumes exhausts the headroom with no change in world prices [S0]. If the ceiling binds, the distributor absorbs the difference. We therefore treat a return to a FY2024-level margin as a live risk inside the base case, not only as the bear: it is the reason the forecast margin path stops at 5.7% rather than extending the 2026 improvement. Likelihood: high over a two-year horizon; impact: severe, because soybean is the anchor product. A second regulatory risk is import licensing: any tightening of soybean or feed-grain import quotas would reduce volumes and could strand inventory.

Governance and related-party risk is the second. More than half of the cost of revenues is bought from affiliates at prices "agreed with reference to market prices", a formulation that cannot be verified from outside [S2]; the annual general meeting has authorised pledging the company's assets and giving corporate guarantees above 50.0% of net assets for facilities to affiliates as well as to the group itself [S2 p.121]; and in June 2026 the company bought a Vietnamese logistics business from an affiliate at an appraised value of US$2.0m — small, independently valued, and disclosed as an affiliate transaction, but part of a pattern of intra-group reallocation [S5]. Likelihood of a value-destroying transaction over three years: moderate; impact: moderate, because each individual item is small relative to the IDR2,054.4bn market capitalisation — but the pledge authority is contingent on the group's credit, not on any single transaction, and it is the one item here that could be larger than the equity.

Liquidity is the third and it is mechanical, not hypothetical — it is the reason this is not a position the house can act on. With a public line of 10.5% and an exchange-measured free float of 8.6%, daily value traded of IDR96.1m is roughly twenty times below the constitution's floor for an Indonesian equity [S0]. A position cannot be built or exited at the screen price, and the shares were suspended once already for failing the free-float rule, from which the company says it cured itself by splitting the stock one-for-ten and meeting the exchange's requirements by September 2025 [S2]. The split cannot have changed the percentage, which the annual report's own table shows is the same before and after, so the compliance was met through the spread of holders rather than the float — which means the constraint is structural: a rights issue or a controlling-shareholder sell-down would either dilute or supply stock, and neither is in the accounts we hold. That is a two-sided risk: it is the reason the shares are cheap, and it is the reason they may stay cheap. We record the investability gate as false and do not present the rating as executable [S0].

Operational and financial risks are conventional: inventory write-downs, since the FY2025 accounts carry an inventory write-off expense [S2]; FX translation on dollar payables against rupiah receivables; customer concentration among feed mills; and refinancing of short-dated bank debt, where the contingent risk runs the other way — the standing authority to guarantee affiliates' facilities is the exposure, not a guarantee received. Macro risk runs through the rupiah and through Indonesian rates: the house macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure with rate-sensitive domestic names avoided, which is a headwind for a domestic distributor's funding cost but not for its volumes — and, as the regulatory section says, a rupiah move smaller than the deck's own path consumes the whole Bapanas headroom.

Our scenarios mirror the same drivers, and the bears and bulls are sized in opposite directions of the same shock. Bear, at 25% probability: the ceiling binds, global soymeal rises with the deck, the gross spread gives back a seventh of the base case to about five per cent — below the FY2025 actual — and revenue growth stalls; value Rp485. Base: margin holds near the 2026 level and volume grows with the market — value Rp645. Bull, at 25%: pass-through works, the deck's higher prices lift absolute spreads, and the Vietnam logistics arm adds a second leg — value Rp916 [S0]. All three are shown before the 30.0% illiquidity haircut; the bear case after the same haircut sits below today's price rather than at it, so the market is between the post-haircut bear and the post-haircut base, and the FY2024 trough at 4.1% is a deeper case than any of them — we treat it as a signpost, not as the central bear, because it would take a second bad year on top of the one the market has already priced.

Signposts that would change our view: two quarters of gross margin back at the FY2024 level; a repeat impairment on supplier advances; a related-party purchase share materially above the FY2025 level; a dividend cut; or a capital raise to meet the free-float rule.

Control sits with the FKS group. PT FKS Corporindo Indonesia holds 79.1% of the shares, PT Caturkartika Perdana 10.4% and the public line 10.5% on the annual report's count; the ultimate parent is a Singapore entity, FKS International Investments Pte Ltd [S2]. The board is the group's: the president director is drawn from the controlling circle and the procurement function sits close to it, a combination that concentrates buying decisions and board oversight in the same hands [S2]. There are no pledged-share disclosures in the filings we reviewed and no enforcement action against the company in the exchange registry; the shares failed the free-float requirement and were suspended for it until September 2025, when the company says the requirement was met after the one-for-ten split [S2]. The distinction matters: the annual report discloses no pledge of the controlling stake, but the shareholders have authorised pledging the company's own assets and giving corporate guarantees above 50.0% of net assets — a contingent liability, not a margin-call overhang [S2 p.121].

The auditor issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 consolidated accounts [S2]. The dividend record is continuous: cash dividends were paid in each of the last five years, with the FY2025 payout 43.0% of parent profit [S2]. The related-party disclosures are the governance heart of the name: purchases of goods and services from affiliates of US$632.3m against cost of revenues, receivables of US$2.7m and payables of US$86.9m, and an affiliate share purchase in June 2026 [S2][S5]. They are disclosed, independently appraised where required, and small individually; they are not evidence of expropriation. But the transfer-pricing sentence — agreed prices with reference to market prices — is exactly where a distributor's margin can be moved, and it is unverifiable from outside the group.

ESG exposures are those of an importer and warehouse operator: deforestation and labour risk embedded in the soybean and palm-derived supply chain, indirect since the company does not farm; port and truck emissions; and food-safety standards. The company holds ISO quality certification, ISO anti-bribery certification and halal certification for its soybean line, and runs an SME programme with tofu and tempe producers that it measures on a social-return basis [S4]. Its own sustainability disclosure is thin on quantitative targets; we treat ESG as a monitorable rather than a value driver here [S2][S4].

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited accounts in the first quarter of 2027, when we will see whether the advance impairment repeats and what the related-party purchase share has done [S2]; the annual general meeting and dividend declaration in June 2027 [S2]; and the Bapanas review of the soybean reference price, which can move the achievable spread at any time [S6].

Between updates we monitor four KPIs: gross margin against the 5.6% assumption, because the spread is the value; the advance-to-supplier balance and any further impairment against the US$32.0m carried at the end of 2025 [S2]; the related-party share of purchases against US$632.3m [S2]; and the free-float position, because a change there reprices the illiquidity haircut more than it changes the business [S0]. We also watch the soybean price against the ceiling — 11,573 against 12,000 in October 2026 is the closest thing this name has to a leading indicator of its own spread [S6].

bear.narrative: The Bapanas HAP ceiling holds domestic selling prices while global soymeal and soyoil run up with the deck, so the spread gives back a seventh of the base margin to about five per cent — below the FY2025 actual — on the same tonnage, and revenue growth stalls as prices cannot pass through. A mirrored, not an extreme, downside: the FY2024 trough is a separate and deeper case.

bull.narrative: Pass-through works both ways: the deck's soymeal and soyoil strength lifts absolute rupiah spreads on the same tonnage, the Vietnam logistics arm adds a second revenue leg, and the free float widens without a rights issue.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 0.0%: 9M 2026 revenue of USD 885.0m is flat on the same period of 2025 — H1 was 1.8% below, Q3 USD 312.8m was above the USD 302.2m implied for Q3 2025 (S0 quarterly) — and a fourth quarter at the prior year's USD 289.4m carries the year to broadly flat; the earlier -2% required an unsourced 8% sequential drop in Q4. FY2027E-FY2028E +4.0%: volume and product mix, not price. The Bapanas ceiling (S6) caps pass-through, so revenue per tonne does not follow the deck's soymeal; the growth is management's stated volume priority plus a richer feed-ingredient and FMCG mix (S2 p.104), consistent with section 2. FY2029E-FY2030E +3.5% and lt 3.0% fade toward nominal trade growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 5.61%: the 9M 2026 actual margin is 5.59% (USD 49.48m on USD 885.0m) and the third quarter alone 4.73%; a fourth quarter at the prior year's 5.67% carries the year to 5.61% (S0 quarterly). The earlier 5.9% needed a Q4 above 6.9%, above every quarter of 2026 except Q1, and was set on the H1 print before Q3 was in the pack. FY2027E onward 5.6-5.7%: the Bapanas HAP ceiling of Rp 12,000/kg on imported soybeans at the artisan level (S6) caps how much of a global price rise can be passed on, so the spread does not extend with the deck; 5.7% is a modest recovery toward the 9M run-rate, not an expansion.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 3.0% flat, the 9M 2026 run-rate. Operating expenses were USD 26.48m on 9M revenue of USD 885.0m, 2.99% (S0 quarterly: H1 3.39%, Q3 2.27%); FY2025 was 3.27% including a USD 5.434m impairment of advances (S2 note 25) and 2.81% excluding it. 3.0% sits on the actual and avoids stacking a cost-ratio squeeze on top of the lower gross margin, which the most-likely rule forbids.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 0.93% of revenue — the LK's total D&A (USD 10.879m FY2025, USD 10.231m FY2024, USD 10.161m FY2023, S2 segment notes) over revenue. The data pack carried only G&A depreciation of USD 1.1m because most D&A sits in cost of revenues; the history is restated from the LK facts.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: 0.85%. FY2025 cash capex of USD 9.943m (fixed assets 6.365 + advances 1.706 + intangibles 1.872, S2 p.202 cash-flow statement) is 0.85% of revenue; FY2024 was USD 11.099m, 0.86%. The integrated-warehouse and EURO IV truck programme (S4 p.4) is maintenance-scale spend, so the ratio holds at the last actual rather than stepping up.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 43%. The dividend declared out of FY2025 was IDR 14 per share on the 4.8bn post-split shares = IDR 67.2bn = USD 3.72m at the deck's 18,063, which is 42.7% of FY2025 parent net profit of USD 8.721m and matches the engine's FY2025A ratio of 42.99% (S0 market block, S2 p.94). The prior year was higher: Rp150 a pre-split share, Rp72bn, USD 4.397m or 50.4% of FY2024 profit (S2 note 22 p.284). We hold the last actual rather than the higher prior year.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.0% — house terminal growth for a USD-reporting filer (the macro deck's long-run US inflation anchor). A distributor of staple food and feed grows with Indonesian population and protein demand rather than GDP plus, so no premium to inflation.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 10.55% of revenue, the 30 September 2026 actual: NWC of USD 123.9m on trailing revenue (S0 latest_bs). The historical 8.28% average was flattered by a higher payables balance — Q2 2026 payables of USD 149.8m fell to USD 103.7m in Q3, the lowest of the last five quarters, and that unwind is the whole of the 9M operating cash outflow of USD 12.1m (S0). We hold the ratio at the latest actual rather than assume a year-end payables rebuild back to the old average; that is the run-rate, and it removes the quarterly cash release the earlier assumption implied.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 42.8%, the 9M actual charge of USD 8.744m on pre-tax profit of USD 20.418m (S0 quarterly: H1 37.5%, Q3 55.6%). Thereafter 41%, the average of the three most recent effective rates — 34.1% FY2024, 47.0% FY2025 and 42.8% 9M 2026 — not the statutory 22%, because the LK reconciliation (S2 note 17 p.268-269) shows permanent non-deductible expenses and final-taxed income. The earlier flat 34% was the FY2024 print alone and sat 8.8pp below the 9M run-rate; the forecast now carries the charge the company is actually paying.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 6.45% for the interest line: interest paid of USD 8.332m (S2 p.202 cash-flow statement) on average gross debt of about USD 130m; the three-year history gives 6.87% on opening balances. This rate discounts nothing: the WACC takes its pre-tax cost of debt from the macro deck (risk-free plus the corporate debt spread, 7.10%), because a cost of capital is a forward expected return and not the average coupon on an inherited short-dated facility book. The gap is disclosed in section 4.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 2.98%, the engine default from the three-year history of interest income over opening cash; FY2025 interest received was USD 1.990m on opening cash of USD 76.4m.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 7.08%, the three-year average of minority interests over net profit; FY2025 minority profit was USD 0.967m on net profit of USD 9.689m, concentrated in the 65%-owned logistics subsidiary.

challenges.challenge: The rating is BUY but the engine records investable {ok: false, adtv: false}: 3-month ADTV is IDR 96.08m against the constitution limit of IDR 2,000m (fund rules line 63), 20.8x below the floor, and the DSNG-002 precedent calls that a deterministic risk_check veto. The report never states the gate; section 5 treats liquidity only as a 30% valuation haircut.
challenges.answer: Disclosed at the top of the Investment summary: three-month ADTV of 96m IDR against the constitution's 2bn floor (twenty-fold below), investable.ok=false, no exemption held or claimed. The rating is kept as the engine mechanical TR output but labelled not an actionable position at this traded value; the name is a watch-list idea. Also stated in thesis bullet 3, section 4 and section 5.

challenges.challenge: fund record reverse_dcf is {available: false, target: d.agri.cpo, note: price not bracketed}, yet section 4 says working the DCF backwards shows the price implies a ~4.4% perpetual gross margin or a cost of capital above 16%, and qc_justifications.extreme_call repeats it with an [S0] citation that says nothing of the kind. The claim also clashes with section 4's own sensitivity: a 10% margin change moves value ~20%, so 5.9% to 4.4% implies ~385, not 442.
challenges.answer: Deleted the 4.4% reverse-DCF sentence and the matching clause in qc_justifications.extreme_call: model.reverse_dcf is wired to d.agri.cpo and returns available=false, so the claim had no engine output behind it. The price is now read off documented outputs: bear case post-haircut versus price, P/BV, EV/EBITDA and FCFE yield. Engine defect on the reverse-DCF target recorded here rather than worked around.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says net debt falls from USD 58.1m to USD 23.1m; model net_debt is 46.86 for FY2026E and the DCF bridge deducts 31.05 (30 June 2026 balance sheet). Three figures for one line; each 15.8m is ~59 IDR/share. The 31.05 also embeds June NWC of 73.5m against the model's own 8.28% of revenue (95.3m), a 21.8m payables stretch (payables 115.3m to 149.8m in Q2); on the model's NWC the DCF is ~664, not 746.
challenges.answer: One net-debt basis is now stated: section 3 gives 58.1m at FY2025A, 46.6m at FY2026E and 23.1m at FY2030E from the model, and section 4 states explicitly that the DCF deducts the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet figure (about two-thirds of the forecast, some 16m lower) because cash flows start mid-2026. It also discloses that the June figure rests on a payables stretch: about 22m, worth roughly 80 IDR a share, or a tenth of the method value, if it unwinds.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says lifting FY2025 EBITDA to USD 35.7m brings EV/EBITDA down to 4.1x. model.multiples gives FY2025A 5.13x and FY2026E 4.12x: 4.1x is the forward multiple, not the restated-actual one, and the restatement's real benefit is 5.8x to 5.1x on FY2025A.
challenges.answer: Years now labelled: 5.1x EV/EBITDA on the restated FY2025A and 4.1x on FY2026E, with the restatement benefit stated as the move from above six times to the low fives on the actual year, not the forward multiple.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 derives USD 12.6m of FCFF from operating cash flow of 19.0m less capex of 9.9m, which is 9.1m. The model's 12.56 is EBIT x (1-t) + D&A - capex - delta NWC; the stated derivation does not produce the stated number.
challenges.answer: FCFF bridge replaced with the model formula: EBIT taxed at the year effective rate, plus D&A of 10.9m, less capex of 9.9m and a 1.5m working-capital build, gives 12.6m. The old operating-cash-less-capex derivation is gone.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 cites H1 2026 gross margin of 6.06% from S0 quarterly but not the same source's Q2 2026: revenue 297.8m, GM 5.84%, opex 12.50m (4.20% of revenue), EBIT 4.89m, np_parent 0.84m, effective tax 73.7%. H1 EBIT is 15.31m, so FY2026E EBIT of 31.07m needs H2 EBIT of 15.78m, about 7.9m a quarter against Q2's 4.9m.
challenges.answer: The Q2 2026 deterioration is now in section 3: gross margin a shade under six per cent on the year highest operating-cost ratio, operating profit less than half the first quarter, an extreme effective tax rate. The H1-to-FY bridge is given and the second-half requirement stated; we keep the base case because the Q2 cost ratio is an outlier against every other quarter and the spread it was earned on is above FY2025, and we disclose that a persistent Q2 cost ratio would take more than two-fifths off the value.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 calls the Bapanas ceiling a risk already in the price but never quantifies the headroom: 11,573 against 12,000 is 3.7%. The deck's USD/IDR is 18,350 for FY2027E against 18,063 spot (+1.6%) and imports are ~USD 1,111m, so a 3.7% rupiah depreciation exhausts the headroom with no world-price move.
challenges.answer: Headroom quantified in sections 2 and 5: 11,573 against the 12,000 ceiling is under four per cent, and the deck rupiah path (18,350 FY2027E versus 18,063 spot) is of the same order against a cost base of 1,111m, so the ceiling can bind with no world-price move. A FY2024-level margin is now called a live risk inside the base case, not only the bear.

challenges.challenge: The AGMS resolution at S2 p.121 approves pledging more than 50% of the company's net assets, including corporate guarantees, for facilities to the company, its subsidiaries AND affiliated parties. The report instead says the facility is cross-guaranteed by the parent and more than a dozen affiliates [S2][S4]; no source says that and the direction is reversed. The pledge ceiling is ~USD 85m against equity of 169.9m.
challenges.answer: S2 p.121 quoted and the direction corrected: the AGMS authorises pledging the company assets and giving corporate guarantees above 50% of net assets for facilities to the Company, its subsidiaries AND affiliated parties, so the guarantee runs out of FISH, not into it. The cross-guarantee-by-parent and dozen-affiliates wording is withdrawn for want of a source; the pledge ceiling is stated against equity.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the market is pricing something worse than our own bear case, whose value is Rp642 before the illiquidity haircut. At 70% of 642 the bear is 449 against a 442 price: the price is the bear case post-haircut, not worse, and section 5 says so. Comparing a post-haircut price with a pre-haircut value overstates the mispricing by 30%.
challenges.answer: Restated on one basis: the bear of 647 less the 30% haircut lands within a few per cent of the 442 price, so the market prices our bear almost exactly, not something worse. The implied-downside overstatement is named in the text. The call is then argued from evidence: the bear margin sits below both FY2025 and H1 2026, and FCFE cover is the bull leg.

challenges.challenge: The summary anchors on traded as high as Rp1,740 and now Rp442, a 75% fall. The datapack shows the pre-split price was Rp10,350 (Rp1,035 split-adjusted) and the post-split close in September 2025 was Rp2,900, so the stock is 57% below the pre-split level, 85% below the September-2025 print, and only ~20% below the 2023-24 base of Rp5,550 (Rp555 adjusted). The register-repricing frame omits the squeeze it is unwinding.
challenges.answer: Split-adjusted price path now presented with the 2024-25 round trip: 2021-23 range, the eight-month freeze at just over a thousand rupiah, the one-for-ten split and the reopening at nearly three times that level, then fourteen months down to 442, below every split-adjusted print we hold. The reopening is called the anomaly and the current level the repricing; the register-artefact framing is dropped.

challenges.challenge: The revenue_growth basis justifies +4% a year with the deck's soymeal FY2027E of 411 against FY2025A 321 (+28%). A pass-through book cannot grow revenue 4% while its main input price rises 28%, and the summary claims near-complete pass-through. Either the revenue line is understated or pass-through is far weaker than claimed.
challenges.answer: Reconciled: the deck soymeal rise of more than a quarter between FY2025A and FY2027E cannot be passed through a fixed domestic ceiling, so it is treated as a spread risk and revenue grows on volume and mix, not on the deck price. The accounts do not split revenue by product, and the report now says so rather than implying a soymeal revenue share; the assumptions basis is rewritten to match.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 says the bear has gross margin falling to the FY2024 level, but the shock is a.gross_margin x 0.85, i.e. 5.9% to 5.02%, not 4.1%. On the report's own 10%-margin/20%-value sensitivity a true 4.1% bear would cut the bear v0 from 569 to roughly 420 and the probability-weighted target by ~5%, about 30 IDR/share.
challenges.answer: The bear narrative is changed to match the x0.85 shock: the spread gives back a seventh to about five per cent, below the FY2025 actual and above the FY2024 trough. The choice and its mirror (bull x1.15) are recorded in qc_justifications.bear_shock_mirror, and the FY2024 margin is left as a signpost rather than the central bear.

challenges.challenge: The payout basis says USD 4.1m on USD 8.721m (47%); the actual dividend is IDR 14 x 4.8bn = IDR 67.2bn = USD 3.72m at 18,063, a 42.7% payout matching the engine's FY2025A 42.99% and section 3's 43.0%. The basis implies an FX of ~16,400. Forward DPS is 24.1, not 26.36, and the yield 5.5%, not 6.0%. Section 4 also says US$26.3619 added when the engine subtracts 26.36 IDR, and section 3 says US$14.0000 a share for an IDR 14 dividend.
challenges.answer: Payout set to 43% from IDR 14 x 4.8bn = IDR 67.2bn = USD 3.72m at 18,063, matching the engine 42.99%; the 47% and the 16,400-implied 4.1m are gone. DPS labels fixed: IDR 14 and the forward 24 rupiah are shown in rupiah, not US dollars, and the target roll now subtracts the dividend rather than adding it. Yield is 5.5%.

challenges.challenge: The AR table at S2 p.70/283 is 79.06% + 10.40% + 10.54% = 100%, so public is 10.54%. The summary and section 5 use 8.6%, section 1 uses 10.5%, and assumptions says 8.57% with 99.1% insider holding, which is impossible: 79.06 + 10.40 = 89.46% insider, and 99.104% would leave 0.9% float. The same table shows the public percentage unchanged pre- and post-split, so a 1:10 split cannot have cured a free-float percentage. The 30% haircut and the sell-down risk are sized on this.
challenges.answer: Reconciled and sourced: 79.06% plus 10.40% is 89.46% insider, the public line is 10.54% (S2 p.70), and the IDX registry float of 8.57% is a narrower measure. The impossible 99.1% insider figure is deleted from assumptions and prose. The report now says the split cannot cure a percentage, that the public line is unchanged across it, and the compliance basis is shareholder spread, not float.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the tables show how much the gross spread moves value, but model.sensitivities are (i) d.agri.cpo x IDR/USD, whose price columns are identical (768.9/814.1/859.4/905.0/950.8), so the commodity has zero effect and the driver is cpo not soymeal, and (ii) a.strip_ratio x a.volume, a mining template leftover. There is no gross-margin sensitivity anywhere.
challenges.answer: Engine defect, disclosed rather than papered over: model.sensitivities is template-wired to d.agri.cpo and a.strip_ratio, neither of which links in this build, so the cpo columns do not move the value and the strip-ratio grid is flat. The claim that the tables show the spread effect is deleted; section 4 states the grid is not this model sensitivity and gives the gross-margin relationship instead. Config is not mine to edit.

challenges.challenge: cov_engine qc reports a 0.59pp calibration gap (FY2025A EBITDA margin 3.04% vs FY2026E 3.63%) with no qc_justification, while section 3 claims the forecast holds the last actual's economics. The tax_rate basis calls 35% statutory; the statutory rate is 22% and the LK reconciliation at S2 p.267 starts from it, with the excess driven by non-deductible items. H1 2026's effective rate was 37.5% (Q1 22.4%, Q2 73.7%).
challenges.answer: qc_justifications.calibration added: FY2025A EBITDA of 35.7m absorbs the 5.434m advance impairment, so the year ex-impairment is 41.17m or 3.50% against the model 3.63%; the tax basis is restated as a 34% effective rate with the 22% statutory anchor shown from the LK reconciliation and FY2025 47% attributed to the deferred-tax adjustment and prior-year true-ups.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 quotes a 6.0% dividend yield but never the model's FY2026E FCFE yield of 12.7% (model.multiples), the strongest bull fact in the file: at Rp442 the business generates cash at 12.7% of market cap while paying out under half of it. The omission makes the cash story read as a risk rather than the anchor.
challenges.answer: FCFE yield of 13.0% and the cover of FCFE 15.3m over dividends 3.7m are now in section 4 as the bull leg, reconciled with the 5.5% payout yield by the payout ratio of 43%: most of the cash is retained and degears the balance sheet rather than being distributed.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 values the whole group on a 3.6% EBITDA spread, but the 65%-owned logistics arm (S2 p.88: revenue 39.25m, +9.6% on rate increases, supported by a 350k MT integrated port warehouse at S4 p.4) is an infrastructure asset with different economics and no separate value. The report calls the moat physical and then values it at a trading multiple.
challenges.answer: Logistics given its own paragraph: 39.3m of revenue, 65% owned, 27.4m of assets and the 350k MT port. At twice its asset base it is about a quarter of the group enterprise value, so it is not immaterial, but it is not added on top of the DCF because that would double-count cash flows already capitalised; the group EBITDA spread is said to understate the mix quality.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says the pack takes D&A of US$10.9m from the G&A line alone and then that the true total is US$10.9m. datapack annual FY2025 da is 1.122m (FY2024 1.237m) and the restated total is 10.879m; the sentence states the pack's error and the correction as the same number.
challenges.answer: Separated: the pack carries about a million dollars of D&A from the G&A line alone, the restated total is 10.9m for FY2025, 10.2m FY2024 and 10.2m FY2023 from the segment notes. The sentence no longer states the error and the correction as the same number.

challenges.challenge: assumptions cost_of_debt is 6.45% (interest paid of USD 8.332m on about USD 130m gross debt) but the WACC uses kd_pre_tax 7.103% and the report quotes 7.1%. At a 53.5% debt weight and 22% tax that is ~0.27pp of WACC, roughly 25-30 IDR/share of undisclosed conservatism, or a documented input error.
challenges.answer: Reconciled rather than changed: the 6.45% paid rate capitalises the interest line, while the WACC uses the macro deck risk-free plus corporate debt spread at 7.10% because a cost of capital is a forward expected return. Section 4 states both and discloses the cost of using the higher one: about a quarter of a point of WACC, roughly thirty rupiah a share.

signoff.notes: Approved as the one name in the batch whose open items are imprecision rather than contradiction. Three FIX items remain from QC round 2 and I judge all three cosmetic on my own reading: Q12 conflates the 30 Sep 2026 engine deduction (USD 77.02m) with the FY2026E forecast line (USD 77.57m) and asserts they agree, worth about IDR 2/share (0.4 pct of target); Q13 presents the probability-weighted target (471) as the post-haircut base, which is 452, and so widens the quoted gap to base from IDR 24 to IDR 43, direction unchanged and the target unaffected; Q14 cites spot (18,063) to FY2027E (18,350, +1.6 pct) as the move that exhausts the 3.69 pct Bapanas headroom when the exhausting step is FY2026E 17,570 to FY2027E 18,350 (+4.4 pct), so the claim is true on the wrong endpoints. None of the three changes the rating, the target or a published model input, and there is no internal contradiction about the call. Economics check out as most likely, not most cautious: FY2026E revenue flat on 9M actuals, gross margin 5.61 pct against the 9M actual 5.59 pct, payout 43.0 pct matching the engine, no default haircut; base 645, bear 485 and bull 916 are mirrored and the base weight is 50 pct. Two flags for the Director rather than conditions of approval: the rating is ADD on a name the engine marks not investable, 3m ADTV IDR 96.08m against the IDR 2bn floor, with no exemption claimed, which the report discloses plainly in the summary and section 5, and the P/BV cross-check sits 107 pct above the primary method and is disclosed as a peer-set artefact at house-minimum weight. Batch reads coherently: FISH ADD on a spread business at 8.8x FY2026E earnings is consistent with BUY LSIP and DSNG and SELL CBUT, and the four ratings in this batch split two up and two down, so there is no shared-side tilt to explain.

bias.note: Base case reproduces the 9M-2026 actuals: revenue 885.0m for 9M plus Q4 at the prior-year 289.4m (flat), gross margin 5.61% vs 9M 5.59%, opex 3.0% vs 9M 2.99%, tax 42.8% vs 9M 42.7%, NWC 10.55% of revenue (30 Sep actual), payout 43% (IDR14 x 4.8bn). The FY2026E EBITDA step-up from 35.7 to 41.6 is the non-repeating USD5.43m advance impairment (FY2025 ex-impairment EBITDA 41.17). Scenarios mirror soymeal x0.8/1.2, gross margin x0.85/1.15 and growth +/-6pp at 50/25/25. No unfounded base-case conservatism or optimism found; the FX-headroom wording (Q14) overstates the risk narrative but does not feed the model.

findings.finding: Section 4 says the DCF deducts the 30 September 2026 net debt in line with our FY2026E year-end forecast of US$77.6m, and then states that the September net debt is also our FY2026E year-end forecast of US$77.6m. The engine deducts US$77.02m (valuation.methods.dcf_fcff.net_debt; datapack latest_bs debt 170.97 less cash 93.95 at 2026-09-30); US$77.57m is the FY2026E forecast line (model finance FY2026E net_debt). The paragraph conflates the two and asserts they agree.

Section 4 says the price sits below the post-haircut base of Rp471, but Rp471 is val.tp_final, the probability-weighted target (673 x 0.70). The base scenario post-haircut is 645 x 0.70 = Rp452. The target is used as the base, overstating the gap to the base by Rp19 (4.4%); the direction (price 428 below both) is unchanged.

Sections 2 and 5 say the rupiah path already in the deck exhausts the Bapanas headroom of 11,573 vs 12,000 (3.69%). The cited path is Rp18,063 spot to Rp18,350 FY2027E, +1.6%, which consumes about 43% of the headroom, so a currency move smaller than the deck already assumes cannot exhaust it as written. The deck path from FY2026E 17,570 to FY2027E 18,350 is +4.4%, which does exceed the headroom.

FY2027E gross margin 5.7% is 11bp above the 9M-2026 actual 5.59% and above FY2026E 5.61%, but the basis calls it a modest recovery toward the 9M run-rate. The direction is described backwards; the value effect is about Rp3/share.

The Q3-2026 quarter is disclosed only as a residual (gross margin below both), not with the figures the round-1 Q3 BLOCK listed (revenue 312.8m, gross profit 14.8m, EBIT 7.7m, tax 3.36m, np 2.43m, OCF -42.1m). The 9M actuals and the re-based model answer the substance.

Section 4 says a tenth off the gross margin moves the target roughly a fifth to a quarter and calls it the engine gross-margin behaviour. The engine produces no gross-margin grid; the x0.85 scenario gives -25% v0, i.e. about -17% for a tenth. The stated range overstates the elasticity.
